ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a single-loop AC circuit, with a voltage source 100cos(ωt) on the left. The top of the loop from left to right is connected in sequence to a 1Ω resistor and a 1H inductor; the right vertical branch is a 1Ω resistor. The label V2 is connected across the two ends of the series combination of the top 1Ω resistor and 1H inductor, and the label V1 is connected across the two ends of the right-side 1Ω resistor. Reasoning: The three components are in the same series loop, so let the loop current phasor be I. The voltage on the right-side 1Ω resistor is V1 = I·1, so V1 is in phase with I. The equivalent impedance of the top 1Ω resistor and 1H inductor is 1 + jω, therefore V2 = I(1 + jω). Therefore the magnitude of the phase difference of V2 relative to V1 is |arg(1 + jω) - arg(1)| = tan^(-1)(ω). The problem states that the magnitude of this phase difference is π/4, therefore tan^(-1)(ω) = π/4, giving ω = tan(π/4) = 1 rad/s.

raw_record.question_text: In the circuit shown, the positive angular frequency \(\omega\) (in radians per second) at which the magnitude of the phase difference between the voltages \(V_1\) and \(V_2\) equals \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) radians, is _____.

method.method_draft: After identifying from the image that all three elements are in one series loop, assign the loop current phasor I. Since V1 is across the right 1 Ω resistor, V1 = I·1 and has the same phase as I. Since V2 is across the top 1 Ω resistor plus 1 H inductor, V2 = I(1 + jω). Therefore the phase difference magnitude between V2 and V1 is |arg(1+jω) - arg(1)| = tan^{-1}(ω). Set tan^{-1}(ω)=π/4 and solve for positive ω, giving ω=1 rad/s.
